title: Progressive-JPEG bit-plane memory: fetch only needed precision
idea: Satellite and web imagery stream progressive bit planes so receivers stop when good enough. Store tensors bit-plane-sliced across columns (sign/exponent plane first, then mantissa planes); each read requests only the top N planes and only those columns are sensed and sent.
why: Most inference reads need 2-4 effective bits of a 16-bit value; energy per access scales with planes fetched, ~4-8x lower, ~10x with shared block exponents.

title: Bit-plane progressive fetch stops when precision suffices
idea: Eliminate low-order bits from the bus: store tensors transposed into bit-planes and fetch sign/exponent/MSB planes first; the consumer's datapath signals 'enough' as soon as the result (e.g., top-k ordering or a dot-product bound) can no longer change, and the remaining planes are never sent.
why: Data movement is 20-25% of accelerator power: on LLM decode ~40-60% of mantissa bits are provably unnecessary per operation, cutting bytes moved ~1.5-2x without fixed quantization loss.
note: Exact early termination on bounds (top-k) is the non-obvious part; bit-plane layout costs write/compute overhead.

title: Bit-plane memory layout for progressive-precision fetch
idea: MINIFY bits moved by storing tensors bit-plane by bit-plane (all MSBs together, then the next plane, and so on), so an accelerator fetches only the top N planes that the current layer or token needs.
why: Data-movement energy and effective capacity: 2-4x fewer bits moved for inference, with precision chosen per access.
note: Bit-plane / progressive-precision layouts are published; software and FPGA demo easy.

title: Paper airplane: bit-plane layout so reads fetch only needed precision
idea: A paper airplane flies with only what it needs: weights are stored transposed into bit-planes, so a 4-bit inference pass reads only the top 4 planes of FP16 weights over the link. Implemented as a controller and layout change on an FPGA prototype.
why: Data-movement energy and bandwidth: 2-4x fewer bits moved per inference, and one stored copy serves many precisions.
note: Bit-plane and any-precision weight layouts already published.

title: Compute embeddings from hashes instead of storing terabyte tables
idea: Recommendation embedding tables are terabytes of mostly cold rows hit by random gathers. Replace lookup with deep-hash embedding: k hashes of the ID feed a small on-accelerator MLP that synthesizes the vector, while only the hottest ~1% of IDs stay in an explicit cache.
why: Table memory falls 100-1000x and random-gather traffic disappears; trades compute and some accuracy.
note: Known art (DHE, TT-Rec); 100x+ recsys table shrink if accuracy holds, trading compute for DRAM.

title: Compressed-sensing readout makes selector-less crossbars usable
idea: The cheapest possible cell is a two-terminal resistor at a wire crossing with no transistor or selector, but sneak paths forbid single-cell reads. Read a whole 1k x 1k tile with pseudo-random row voltage patterns, measure column currents, and let a decoder in the interface chiplet solve the linear system (with sparse coding and block parity) to recover every bit.
why: 8-16 stacked BEOL crossbar layers at 4F^2 with 2-3 masks each could approach ~100x cheaper per GB; trades latency (us tile decode), energy and endurance.
note: Decoding summed currents needs high ADC precision against IR drop; resistive endurance not DRAM-class.

title: IBM MXT fixed: compression lives in the CXL link, not the core
idea: IBM's Memory eXpansion Technology (2000) doubled effective capacity with hardware compression but died from decompression latency on the CPU critical path, a large L3 requirement and OS changes. Put a 2-4 ns base-delta/zero-run compressor with a metadata cache inside the CXL memory controller, present the OS a fixed larger capacity, and compress only far-tier lines so hot data never pays the latency.
why: Do DRAM's job with less, and link energy: server data typically compresses 1.5-2.5x, so 33-60% fewer DRAM bits for the same capacity and fewer bits crossing the link.

title: Mycorrhizal memory sharing: gradient-driven DRAM lending between servers
idea: Servers on a CXL switch fabric run a decentralized 'wood-wide-web' protocol: each node advertises a scalar gradient (free memory minus pressure), and pages flow one hop at a time from surplus to starved neighbours, the way mycorrhizal fungi move sugar from sunlit to shaded trees. There is no global allocator; borrowed pages carry a lease that is recalled when the donor's gradient flips.
why: Usable supply: datacenters strand ~20-30% of installed DRAM; reclaiming half of it equals ~10-15% more effective DRAM supply with zero new wafers.
note: Decentralized gradient diffusion of pages; pooling itself widely pursued.

title: Reclaimed server DIMMs reborn as CXL memory pools
idea: Substitute new DRAM purchases with DDR4/DDR5 DIMMs pulled from decommissioned servers: a small team builds an FPGA or off-the-shelf CXL-controller card holding 8-16 used DIMMs, screens them with an on-card pattern tester, and sells them as CXL Type-3 capacity tiers.
why: Cost per bit and scarcity: reused bits cost ~10-20% of new ones and add supply with zero fab capex during the 4x price spike.
note: Hyperscalers already reuse DDR4 behind CXL; supply bounded by retirement volume.

title: Second-life DRAM: retired server DIMMs reborn as CXL pools
idea: Eliminate new wafers for the capacity tier: strip DDR4/DDR5 chips from decommissioned servers, screen with burn-in and row-hammer tests, and mount them behind CXL Type-3 controllers that translate protocol and map out weak rows.
why: Huge volumes of DRAM are retired yearly; reusing it as a slower tier raises usable supply with zero fab capex and spares new DDR5/HBM for hot data, at ~5-10x lower cost/bit than today's 4x contract price.
note: Hyperscalers already reuse DDR4 behind CXL; chip-level harvesting adds screening cost.

title: Secondary-market DDR4 reborn in CXL memory expansion boxes
idea: Box: reclaimed DDR4 DIMMs x standard x standard x CXL controller with per-rank ECC remap and aging-aware refresh x refurbished chassis x refurbishment line. DDR4 from decommissioned servers is tested, graded and re-hosted behind CXL controllers that hide its latency for tier-2 data.
why: Supply: capacity with zero new wafers; tens of PB of DDR4 retire each year; cost per GB ~20-30% of new DDR5.
note: Retired DDR4 behind CXL already piloted by hyperscalers; solid but known.

title: Cheap short-living objects: retired server DDR4 reborn as CXL memory
idea: TRIZ #27 Cheap short-living objects: hyperscalers retire millions of DDR4 DIMMs. Collect, retest and bin them, then mount 8-16 on each CXL Type-3 card built around a 28 nm controller, as a cheap cold tier for KV cache and page cache. (No new fab: only existing trailing-node capacity.)
why: Usable supply: reuses DRAM that already exists, at ~10-20% of new DRAM cost per GB and zero wafer starts.
